title: Who is she coming
greek: Chi è questa che vèn; Lat. Quae est ista quae progreditur
short: The opening question echoes the Song of Songs: 'Who is she that looketh forth as the morning?' (6:10; Vulgate 6:9).
body: Cavalcanti's 'Chi è questa che vèn' recalls the Vulgate's 'Quae est ista quae progreditur quasi aurora consurgens' (Song of Songs 6:9; KJV 6:10, 'Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?'), and also 3:6 ('Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness'). The Rossetti Archive and other commentators point to the Song of Songs and to Isaiah 63:1 ('Who is this that cometh from Edom'). The Song's verse was read in the liturgy of the Virgin, so the lady arrives with Marian and scriptural associations.

title: the sonnet and its translator
short: Cavalcanti's sonnet 'Chi è questa che vèn, ch'ogn'om la mira' (Rime IV), here in Rossetti's 1861 translation, under his own title.
body: Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255-1300), Dante's 'first friend', was the most philosophical poet of the dolce stil novo. This sonnet, perhaps of the late 1270s (the Rossetti Archive's tentative date), is his best-known poem of praise; it is clearly indebted to Guinizzelli's sonnet 'Io voglio del ver la mia donna laudare'. The lady is seen in public, 'ch'ogn'om la mira' (whom every man gazes at), a scene Dante develops in 'Tanto gentile'. Rossetti's title 'A Rapture concerning his Lady' is his own; it appears in The Early Italian Poets (1861). His translation follows the Italian line by line.

title: the air tremulous with light
short: Translates 'che fa tremar di chiaritate l'âre': who makes the air tremble with brightness.
body: 'Chiaritate' is the scholastic claritas, radiance, one of the attributes of beauty and of glorified bodies in medieval theology. The lady's light acts on the very medium through which she is seen, in line with medieval optics, in which light passes through the air to the eye. Rossetti's 'tremulous with light' is among his most successful lines and preserves the sense that the atmosphere itself responds to her. Ezra Pound, who translated Cavalcanti repeatedly, prized this luminous, shimmering quality in Cavalcanti.

title: Love himself
short: Translates 'e mena seco Amor': she leads Love with her. Love is personified, as throughout the Italian lyric.
body: Amor, personified as a lord or companion, is a stock figure of the Italian love lyric and of the Vita Nuova, where Love appears to Dante in dreams and speaks. Here he walks at the lady's side, as if her attendant. Rossetti's rhetorical question ('And at whose side is Love himself?') breaks the Italian sentence differently: in Cavalcanti the whole quatrain is a single question ending at 'sospira'.

title: speechlessness and sighs
short: Cavalcanti: 'sì che parlare / null'omo pote, ma ciascun sospira', so that no man can speak, but each one sighs.
body: The beholders are reduced to sighs, the involuntary sign of love's effect on the spirits. Rossetti adds 'infinite', heightening the effect. The motif of speechlessness returns at once in line 6 ('I may not speak thereon') and governs the poem's end, where the mind cannot know her. Dante's 'Tanto gentile' (in the archive as 'My lady looks so gentle and so pure') reworks the same motif of the mute tongue and the sigh.

sources.cite: Guido Cavalcanti, Rime, ed. Domenico De Robertis (Turin: Einaudi, 1986), no. IV, with commentary
Robert Pogue Harrison, 'Saved by a Vision of Beatrice', New York Review of Books, 26 May 2011

anchor: how she looks round from left to right
title: when she turns her eyes
greek: O Deo, che sembra quando li occhi gira
short: Cavalcanti: 'O Deo, che sembra quando li occhi gira!', O God, what she seems when she turns her eyes!
body: Rossetti turns the exclamation 'O Deo' into 'Ah me!' and spells out the turning of the eyes as looking 'from left to right'. The Song of Songs offers a loose parallel in 6:5 (Vulgate 6:4): 'Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me.' The lady's glance, which in medieval love theory sends spirits or rays into the beholder, is the moment of greatest power. The verb 'sembra' (seems, appears) is the same kind of word as Dante's 'pare'.

title: Let Love discourse
short: Cavalcanti: 'dical'Amor, ch'i' nol savria contare', let Love tell it, for I could not recount it.
body: An inexpressibility topos: only Love, the personified power who accompanies her, could describe her effect. 'Discourse' in Rossetti's sense is to speak at length or relate. The poet's incapacity anticipates the sestet, where neither praise nor knowledge suffices. The same deferral of speech to Love appears in the Vita Nuova, where Dante repeatedly says that his tongue cannot express what Beatrice's presence does, and leaves the telling to the sigh or to Love. The topos is old, but in Cavalcanti it carries his recurrent sense that the lover's own faculties are overwhelmed and disabled by love.

sources.cite: Guido Cavalcanti, Rime, ed. Domenico De Robertis (Turin: Einaudi, 1986), no. IV, with commentary

title: benison... graceless
short: Cavalcanti: 'cotanto d'umiltà donna mi pare, / ch'ogn'altra ver' di lei i' la chiam'ira'. Rossetti's 'benison' and 'graceless' interpret a difficult couplet.
body: The Italian says the lady seems so full of 'umiltà' (benign graciousness, not humility in the modern sense) that beside her every other woman 'I call wrath' ('i' la chiam'ira'): others seem harsh or hostile by comparison. Editors have debated the construction and the sense of 'ira'; some modern paraphrases render it as 'wicked' or 'disdainful'. Rossetti replaces umiltà with 'benison' (blessing; OED, benison, n.) and 'ira' with 'graceless', choosing the language of grace and turning the comparison theological.

title: the sestet and rhyme
greek: Non si poria contar la sua piagenza
short: The sestet opens 'Non si poria contar la sua piagenza', her charm could not be recounted; Rossetti's rhymes rearrange Cavalcanti's.
body: Cavalcanti's sonnet rhymes ABBAABBA CDEEDC. Rossetti's octave rhymes ABABBAAB (upon, light, none, infinite; right, thereon, benison, sight) and his sestet CDECDE (said, virtuous, deity; led, us, perfectly), so the English moves differently while keeping fourteen lines and the turn at line 9. 'Piagenza' means pleasingness, charm; Rossetti's 'honour' is a free rendering that stresses dignity rather than delight. The sestet then moves from what cannot be said to what cannot be known.

title: all things virtuous
short: Cavalcanti: 'ch'a le' s'inchin' ogni gentil vertute', every noble power bows to her.
body: 'Vertute' in medieval Italian means power or faculty (Latin virtus, strength) as much as moral virtue: the noble powers of the soul and of nature bow down to her. Rossetti's 'To whom are subject all things virtuous' keeps the hierarchy but leans toward the moral sense. 'Gentil' again denotes stilnovo nobility of heart. The bowing of the powers to the lady is a courtly gesture of homage transferred to abstractions.

title: own her deity
greek: la beltate per sua dea la mostra
short: Cavalcanti: 'e la beltate per sua dea la mostra', and Beauty shows her forth as its goddess.
body: Beauty, personified, displays the lady as its own goddess. 'Own' in Rossetti's line means 'acknowledge'. The bold language of divinity applied to a woman is typical of the stilnovo's quasi-religious praise, and the Rossetti Archive's commentary singles out the poem for treating a mortal woman as a near-transcendent source of grace. It is also the kind of language that later made the tradition suspect to moralists.

anchor: Ne'er was the mind of man so nobly led
title: the limits of the mind
short: Cavalcanti: 'Non fu sì alta già la mente nostra', our mind was never so lofty, i.e. never high enough.
body: The sestet's last tercet turns from praise to epistemology. 'Mente' is the intellect. In Cavalcanti's philosophical canzone 'Donna me prega' love is a passion of the sensitive soul that clouds rational judgement, and the beloved's true form can be grasped only as an abstract idea in the possible intellect; the sonnet's ending reflects that Aristotelian, perhaps Averroist, psychology. Rossetti's 'so nobly led' adds the idea of guidance.

sources.cite: Guido Cavalcanti, Rime, ed. Domenico De Robertis (Turin: Einaudi, 1986), no. IV, with commentary

title: redemption (salute)
short: Cavalcanti: 'e non si pose 'n noi tanta salute', nor was so much salvation (or health) placed in us.
body: 'Salute' means both health and salvation (Latin salus). Rossetti chooses the theological sense and heightens it to 'redemption', linking the poem to the scriptural opening. Dante plays on the same word in the Vita Nuova, where Beatrice's greeting (saluto) brings salute; compare 'Tanto gentile', where her greeting is the centre of the poem. The word thus links praise of the lady with the language of grace and salvation.

title: knowing her
short: Cavalcanti: 'che propiamente n'aviàn canoscenza', that we could properly have knowledge of her.
body: The poem ends not on rapture but on a limit: human minds lack the capacity to know her as she truly is. Harrison and others contrast this note with Dante's 'Tanto gentile', which describes the same public scene but ends with the lady's spirit actually reaching the beholder's soul. Cavalcanti's darker view of love, as an accident that the intellect cannot master, is the background. Rossetti's 'perfectly' renders 'propiamente', in its own proper nature.
